prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level and opened new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a single clean idea, Katori's magic-wavelength trapping that removes the light shift while confining many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and on a decisive demonstration that this idea reaches the accuracy frontier, which is the Ye-group work on strontium. The result is a nameable discovery-level advance in instrumentation: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 confirmed by independent laboratories and by intercontinental comparisons. It already supports tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, searches for dark-matter signatures, relativistic geodesy and the roadmap to redefine the second. The attribution is unusually tidy, with two people whose roles are distinct and well documented, and the maturity is real: more than two decades of development and replication across species and groups. After colleagues' arguments I keep it first, and I now think the committee should treat it as the single-achievement baseline against which two-part packages must justify themselves.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier recognition: the 2012 prize for controlling single ions and the 2005 prize for the frequency comb already cover large parts of the technology stack, so the committee must articulate why the lattice idea is a distinct step rather than a refinement of optical frequency standards. There is also a genuine credit question, since the strontium and ytterbium lattice work involved other leading contributors and a clock is a team product; two names fit the prize rules but may read as narrow. Finally, the formal redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some colleagues may judge the application milestone premature, and a metrology prize can look less like a discovery of nature than neutrino astronomy or a new phase of matter.

responses.point: Ranks IceCube's detection of astrophysical neutrinos (B014) first as the opening of an observational discipline, while noting that large-collaboration credit requires a fair two-name split.
responses.response: I accept that B014 is a real discovery of nature and that it is comparably mature, and I rank it above most of the field. My difficulty is the credit structure you yourself flag: a cubic-kilometre detector is a collaboration of hundreds, and Halzen and Karle are two of several people with a strong claim, so the prize risks an arbitrary cut. By contrast the lattice-clock credit is separable and documented. I would also ask whether the diffuse flux and the NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results are as yet a stable measurement programme or still a source-identification story. I would not oppose B014 as a second part, but I do not think it displaces B015 as the cleaner single case.

responses.point: Puts B015 first because the magic-wavelength lattice turned narrow-line spectroscopy into the most accurate measurements ever made, with Katori proposing and Ye driving performance and many-body integration.
responses.response: I agree on the core and share your first place, but I would qualify two points. The many-body and spin-exchange physics in Ye's later work is real but is not the reason the prize is deserved, and I would keep the citation anchored on the clock concept and its accuracy rather than on later extensions, so it does not invite arguments about Sr versus Yb or about quantum-gas clocks. I would also resist leaning on the redefinition of the second as a justification, because that is a metrology-body decision and a prize should stand on the scientific achievement already demonstrated. If a second part is wanted, your B009 and B032 are strong, but both overlap prior atomic-physics prizes more heavily than the clock does.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED (B039) first and trapped-ion quantum computation (B009) second, as the architectural basis of quantum processors, while recognising that the 2025 prize on circuit macroscopic quantum effects narrows B039's novelty.
responses.response: I take the point that circuit QED is the more consequential platform for quantum processors, and I do not dispute its originality. Where I disagree is that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits sits close enough that a second superconducting-circuit prize within a year would look repetitive, and the credit for B039 is contested by Devoret, Martinis and others outside the list. For B009 the 2012 ion-control prize creates a similar overlap. I do not think quantum-computing impact is the right yardstick by itself: an engineering platform should be recognised when its physics discovery is distinct, and I would be willing to revisit B039 as an alternative if the committee decides the 2025 prize does not preclude it.

responses.point: Ranks fluctuation theorems (B005) first as exact, widely used results on non-equilibrium work and free energy, with Jarzynski and Crooks as the clearest decisive contributors and Evans having a strong claim.
responses.response: The fluctuation relations are elegant and I respect the argument for B005, but the evidence for broad discovery impact is thinner than for the clock: the experimental confirmations are mostly in small systems and biomolecules, and the attribution is exactly the difficulty you describe, since Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles and others have claims that a three-name list will not settle cleanly. I also note that only one member ranked B005 at all, so it has not yet persuaded the room. I would be glad to hear what specific measurement or application you regard as decisive, because for me that would change the ranking more than the theoretical elegance.

responses.point: Prefers B014 on the grounds that it is a clear discovery of nature tying particle physics to astrophysics, with B030 and B039 as his next choices.
responses.response: I understand the appeal of beginning with a discovery of nature, and I regard B014 as a serious candidate, but I would not exclude instrument-driven advances on that basis, since measurement is where most atomic-physics discoveries begin and the clock comparisons are already producing physical bounds. I do share your regard for B030, which is my own second choice, because it combines a theoretical prediction with a prompt experimental discovery. My reservation about B030 is maturity: the origin of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is still debated, and the experimental credit centres on a group whose co-authors are outside the three allowed names.

uncertainties: Whether two names fairly represent the lattice-clock field given contributions from other groups on Sr and Yb, and whether the committee wants to credit by concept (Katori) and performance (Ye) or add a third name.
Whether the committee regards the 2012 single-ion prize and the 2005 comb prize as narrowing the novelty of optical lattice clocks enough to prefer a different configuration.
Whether pairing B015 with a second distinct achievement (for example B014 or B030) would produce a better balanced prize, or only an artificial one given name-count constraints.
Whether the maturity of B030 and the large-collaboration credit for B014 are resolved enough to treat them as peer alternatives.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile with respect to B015, B014, B030 or B018. My documented collaborations (including with Anne L'Huillier, Ursula Keller's group, the Lund attosecond group and storage-ring colleagues) do not involve Katori, Ye or the other credited names on this shortlist, but I work in atomic physics and know the clock community professionally, which the committee may wish to note.
